section_summary: This section traces Japan’s economic conditions from late 1932 into early 1933, including rural debt, yen depreciation, industrial recovery, foreign trade, rising living costs, and unemployment. It contains embassy despatches and report excerpts, Department of Commerce circulars, file notes, and correspondence. The final pages begin a briefing for preliminary talks with Japan before the World Monetary and Economic Conference.

subfiles.title: General Financial and Economic Conditions, August 1932
subfiles.about: Reports rural distress, the falling yen, rising silk prices, Indian cotton tariffs, and foreign securities holdings.
subfiles.summary: The report describes severe farm debt and hunger, a sharp decline in the yen, and a compensating rise in silk prices. It also considers the effects of India’s higher duty on Japanese cotton cloth and records Finance Department estimates of foreign currency securities held by Japanese residents.

subfiles.title: File note for despatch No. 117
subfiles.about: Cross-references Grew’s despatch on Japan’s economic conditions and future contingencies.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to file 894.51/378 for Grew’s despatch No. 117.

subfiles.title: Present Economic Conditions in Japan in Relation to Future Contingencies
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Japan’s finances and economy could sustain its Manchurian policy under military costs, boycott, or financial pressure.
subfiles.summary: Grew examines farm and small business indebtedness, relief legislation, the national debt, yen depreciation, and the apparent short-term improvement in Japanese industry and agriculture. He argues that Japan’s external payments and access to foreign credit remain vulnerable. He then considers the capacity to finance military operations, withstand an economic boycott, and endure sustained financial pressure from abroad.

subfiles.title: General Economic and Financial Conditions, September 1932
subfiles.about: Reviews temporary industrial and farm improvement, yen movement, trade, postal savings, and barriers to economic union with Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Shipping, silk, and cotton spinning improve while military spending clouds the outlook. The report notes postal savings withdrawals and economic obstacles to closer union with Manchuria.

subfiles.title: File note for despatch No. 174
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on continued prosperity in some Japanese industries.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to despatch No. 174 in file 894.00 P.R./59.

subfiles.title: General Economic and Financial Conditions, October 1932
subfiles.about: Reports continuing industrial activity, improved trade, Hokkaido flooding, and a renewed fall in the yen.
subfiles.summary: Industry and trade improve, but Hokkaido suffers flooding and the yen weakens.

subfiles.title: File note for despatch No. 201
subfiles.about: Cross-references Grew’s report on financial affairs, economic conditions, and the budget.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to despatch No. 201 in file 894.51/392.

subfiles.title: Economic Conditions in Japan
subfiles.about: Explains Japan’s rapid but potentially temporary recovery after yen depreciation and government spending.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports rising factory output, exports, silk income, and confidence in banks, while examining exchange rates, bond issues, external payments, and the coming budget. He calls the prosperity artificial and predicts that tariffs, rising domestic costs, taxes, and industrial overexpansion may eventually bring a severe downturn. The recovery could meanwhile help finance military operations in Manchuria.

subfiles.title: File note for Financial and Economic Annual of Japan, 1932
subfiles.about: Records a despatch transmitting two copies of Japan’s 1932 financial and economic annual.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references the despatch transmitting two copies of the annual.

subfiles.title: File note for despatch No. 218
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report attributing Japanese prosperity to yen depreciation and government spending.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to despatch No. 218 in file 894.00 P.R./60.

subfiles.title: General Economic and Financial Conditions, November 1932
subfiles.about: Summarizes strong industrial activity and exports alongside concern about debt-financed spending and further yen depreciation.
subfiles.summary: Textiles, steel, agriculture, and exports benefit from the cheap yen. The report cautions that proposed bond issues could bring inflation.

subfiles.title: File note on the outlook for Japanese prosperity
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report predicting that Japan’s current prosperity may prove short-lived.
subfiles.summary: Notes a forecast of worsening conditions in the second half of the year.

subfiles.title: Internal Economic and Financial Conditions, December 1932
subfiles.about: Reports continued prosperity, rising prices and shares, and proposed stronger exchange controls.
subfiles.summary: Observers warn that the boom may turn downward later in 1933.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan’s living costs and income
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Commerce Department circular finding that prices rose while wages and employment remained weak.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum highlights reduced purchasing power, higher food and fertilizer costs, lower savings income, and persistent unemployment despite industrial expansion.

subfiles.title: Letter enclosing a circular on Japan’s economic situation
subfiles.about: Sends two copies of a circular on higher living costs and lower income in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Moser encloses a circular for use in assessing the effects of yen depreciation.

subfiles.title: Domestic Situation in Japan Aggravated by Increased Living Costs and Lower Income
subfiles.from: V. P. Copping; Far Eastern Section
subfiles.about: Analyzes exchange rates, retail prices, wages, unemployment, and labor disputes in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The circular documents rising living costs after yen depreciation without a matching increase in purchasing power. Farmers gain from higher rice and cocoon prices but face higher production costs and heavy debts. City workers, pensioners, and savers suffer most; factory growth often relies on machinery and overtime rather than new hiring. Wage disputes and unemployment remain serious.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Commerce Department circular
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the circular on Japanese living costs and income.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Moser for the circular and calls it illuminating.

subfiles.title: File note for a report on Japanese industry
subfiles.about: Cross-references a despatch reporting continued prosperity in Japan’s principal industries.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to a despatch on Japan’s industrial boom.

subfiles.title: General Economic and Financial Conditions, January 1933
subfiles.about: Reports continuing industrial prosperity, a stock market decline, and falling raw silk prices.
subfiles.summary: The silk price drop prompts plans to keep filatures closed in February.

subfiles.title: Economic Notes on Japan
subfiles.from: C. K. Moser; Far Eastern Section
subfiles.about: Compiles statistics on Japan’s population, finance, labor, production, prices, and trade.
subfiles.summary: The circular provides figures for American investments, Japan’s debt, budget, currency, production, wages, unemployment, and foreign trade. Detailed tables compare trade with the United States, China, and other major partners, including principal commodities and the effects of exchange rate changes.

subfiles.title: File note for despatch No. 348
subfiles.about: Cross-references a despatch on Japan’s Steel Merger Law.
subfiles.summary: Notes proposed consolidation of government steel mills with five large private companies.

subfiles.title: Japan—Economic Matters
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Labels the following material as confidential Japan economic matters.
subfiles.summary: Confidential cover bears a 1947 return instruction.

subfiles.title: World Monetary and Economic Conference: Preliminary Conversations at Washington—Japan
subfiles.about: Introduces the Japanese delegation and briefs U.S. officials on Japan’s politics and bilateral relations.
subfiles.summary: The briefing begins with a contents list, delegation roster, and biographical notes on Kikujiro Ishii and Eigo Fukai. It then describes the Japanese military’s growing control of government after the Manchurian incident and Inukai’s assassination. The final pages open a historical review of U.S.–Japan relations; that review continues beyond page 159.
